hints: Focus on the words telophase and in one of the nuclei. How many chromosomes have arrived at each pole, and what does a single chromosome look like at that point?
Remember where telomeres are found. How many ends, and therefore how many telomeres, does one single-chromatid chromosome have?
walkthrough:
**Recall what a telomere is**

Think of a chromosome like a short rod. A telomere is the protective cap at the tip.

Every chromosome has two ends, so one chromosome has 2 telomeres.

**Work out chromosomes in one telophase nucleus**

The starting diploid cell has 22 chromosomes. In mitosis, sister chromatids separate in anaphase.

By telophase, each new daughter nucleus receives the full diploid set, so one nucleus contains 22 chromosomes, each made of one chromatid.

**Calculate the telomeres**

Now just multiply chromosomes by telomeres per chromosome:
$$22 \text{ chromosomes} \times 2 \text{ telomeres per chromosome} = 44 \text{ telomeres}$$ 
That matches option B.

options.A: This counts only one telomere per chromosome. Remember each chromosome has two ends, so two telomeres.
options.B: Correct. One nucleus has 22 single-chromatid chromosomes, each with 2 ends, giving 22 x 2 = 44 telomeres.
options.C: There is no biological basis for 66 here. It does not fit 2 telomeres per chromosome for 22 chromosomes.
options.D: 88 would be the total for both daughter nuclei together, or for 22 double-chromatid chromosomes. The question asks for one nucleus in telophase only.
